notes:
I've organised these notes verse by verse, with the page URL after each point. A few things to know first:

- **Sources:** Most come from Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin (which gathers modern evangelical commentators such as Thompson, Selman, Dillard, Hill and Allen), and the older commentaries on Bible Hub and StudyLight (Gill, Ellicott, Matthew Henry, Pulpit Commentary, Trapp, Poole, Barnes).
- **Gaps:** I didn't reach the separate per-verse pages for vv. 13 and 15, so those notes are thinner. I found nothing for Part 3's Catholic, Orthodox or popular-modern-teaching readings (see the end).

---

## Part 1: The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1** – Guzik says Rehoboam turned from God's law once he felt secure. He relied on God while he needed Him, then quickly grew independent from God once he felt secure, leading the whole nation into idolatry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Trapp notes he showed some goodness for his first three years, while he feared losing the kingdom, and turned away once he felt settled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-12.html
- Clarkson (Pulpit Commentary) calls this "the temptation of supposed security": once safe, Rehoboam relaxed his hold on his early convictions. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-12.html
- On Precept Austin, one writer says "forsaking" the law doesn't mean they threw it off entirely (the excerpt breaks off there). Hill reads "all Israel" as every Israelite living in Judah, whether of northern or southern tribal stock. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 2** – Ellicott gives the order of events: For three years Rehoboam and his people continued faithful to the Lord (2Chronicles 11:17); in the fourth year they fell away; and in the fifth their apostacy was punished. He calls "because they had transgressed" the Chronicler's own aside, summing up his whole view of Israel's history. Shishak himself didn't know he was carrying out God's purpose. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-2.htm
- Guzik notes that "unfaithful" is a key word in Chronicles that never appears in Samuel or Kings. Quoting Selman, he says it is the main reason Chronicles gives for the exile. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Constable sees a deliberate echo of Saul: the same word was used of Israel's first king (1 Chr 10:13). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-11.html
- Whitelaw (Pulpit) names two causes. Shishak may have wanted to help Jeroboam, but God's purpose was to punish. Had Rehoboam stayed faithful, Jeroboam's schemes would have failed. Trapp says much the same. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-12.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-12.html

**v. 3** – Ellicott treats the numbers as probably round numbers founded on a rough estimate. He says the three peoples were the foot soldiers. Libyans and Cushites appear together as Egypt's allies in Nahum 3:9. The Sukkites are unknown, though the Septuagint and Vulgate render the name "Troglodytes" (cave-dwellers). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-3.htm
- Older writers disagree about the Sukkites. Poole, Gesenius and Barnes lean toward "tent-dwellers" (Arabs or an African tribe). Benson, Clarke and the Geneva notes prefer cave-dwellers on the Red Sea coast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-3.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-3.html
- Precept Austin's own note: the army was huge, but that is not why Judah fell. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 4** – Guzik says the southern kingdom could have perished only two generations after David. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Matthew Henry says the fortified cities Rehoboam had relied on fell without resistance, which showed the disaster came from the Lord. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-12.html

**v. 5** – Guzik says Shemaiah is the same prophet who stopped Rehoboam from attacking the north (11:1–4). He sees the punishment as matching the sin: This was a correction that matched the offense. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Gill thinks the leaders met in fear, to decide whether to fight Shishak or make peace. The prophet was sent to explain what was happening and call them to repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-12.html
- Whitelaw: God was signalling that He, even more than Shishak, had come against them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-12.html
- Thompson (on Precept Austin) says the verb "abandon" (*azab*) carries special theological weight. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 6** – Guzik: To recognize that the LORD is righteous is also to recognize that we are not. He adds that this repentance began with the leaders. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- De Vries (on Precept Austin) calls "Righteous is Yahweh!" perhaps the key statement of the whole account. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary
- Matthew Henry pictures them admitting they had no one to blame but themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-12.html

**v. 7** – Matthew Henry says the deliverance was partial and lasted only a little while. They reformed but partially, and for a little while, soon relapsing again; and, as their reformation was, so was their deliverance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-12.html
- Precept Austin sums it up as discipline but not destruction. Olley reads "some deliverance" as "a little escape". https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 8** – Guzik quotes Clarke: serving God proved to be perfect freedom, while forsaking Him brought perfect bondage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Clarkson (Pulpit) says God wanted Rehoboam to compare his three good years (11:17) with harsh subjection to Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-12.html
- Barnes: they would learn how light God's rule was next to the heavy yoke of a foreign monarch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-12.htm
- Allen (on Precept Austin) compares this to Jacob's limp, a lasting reminder of the struggle. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 9** – Commentators disagree on whether Jerusalem was taken. Whitelaw cites Bertheau and Keil, who think the plunder implies capture. He also cites Rawlinson, who thinks Rehoboam may have handed over the treasures to save the city, as Hezekiah later did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-12.html
- Trapp says Josephus has Shishak plundering the city, but thinks a large payment is more likely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-12.html
- Spurgeon (on Precept Austin) contrasts God, who asks for a tithe, with "Shishak and Satan", who take everything. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**vv. 10–11** – Guzik says gold shields were useless in battle and showed image winning over substance. The replacement of Solomon's gold shields with Rehoboam's bronze shields in just five years is a vivid picture of how quickly the dynasty declined. He quotes Payne and Morgan on God's people putting up with imitations once they have lost what was real. He also notes that the bronze shields were locked in a guardroom rather than displayed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- Another writer on Precept Austin says the shields kept up an appearance of wealth while hiding Judah's real state. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 12** – This verse is the Chronicler's own; it isn't in Kings (Ellicott, Pulpit). The phrase "conditions were good" is read three ways:
- **There was real goodness left in Judah.** Ellicott takes it this way and says it was an extra reason God spared the land; compare 19:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-12.htm Gill speaks of faithful priests, Levites and ordinary people, comparing Gen 18:31. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-12.html
- **Either goodness or recovering prosperity.** Poole and Benson allow both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-12.htm Matthew Henry includes both too, and adds that we should thank God even for some deliverance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-12.html
- **Deliberately left open.** Dillard says the "good" is never defined. Hill thinks it looks back to the three faithful years. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

Guzik reads this as a further humbling beyond v. 6, still pure mercy, since justice alone would have allowed complete destruction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/

**v. 13** – Gill says that after Shishak left, Rehoboam strengthened Jerusalem further and reigned twelve more years (seventeen in all). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-12.html
- The Restoration Commentary notes that God had forbidden marriage with foreigners, yet Rehoboam's mother was an Ammonite. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-12.html

**v. 14** – Most sources take this as the summary of his reign. Matthew Henry: he was never rightly fixed in his religion. He never prayed for wisdom as Solomon did. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-12.html
- Barnes: his sin was a lack of earnestness and consistency. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-14.html
- Trapp: his good resolutions were flashy and fleeting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/2ch-12.cfm
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) says he kept shifting between God and idols and made no great reforms. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary partly blames his foreign mother's influence for his leaning toward idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-14.html
- Thompson notes that Kings blames the whole nation's idolatry (1 Kgs 14:22–24), while Chronicles focuses on Rehoboam himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

**v. 15** – Trapp says the books of Shemaiah and Iddo no longer exist. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-12.html
- The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary reads the "wars" as border raids and skirmishes rather than open war. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-14.html

**v. 16** – Guzik, quoting Selman, says Chronicles presents Rehoboam as a pattern and an encouragement for the returning exiles. It wants to show the value of repentance and the extent of God's mercy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-12/

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no clear denominational dispute on this chapter. The nearest thing is a difference of emphasis over **whether Rehoboam's humbling (vv. 6, 12) was sincere**:
- Gill (Calvinist Baptist) calls it contrite only "seemingly", since it was merely external. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-12.html
- Wesley's Notes (Arminian), in the only excerpt I could see, say he humbled himself for a season, yet he quickly relapsed into sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-14.html
- Modern evangelicals such as Selman and Mabie stress real mercy as an encouragement to repent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary

This is a matter of emphasis between individual writers, not a recorded tradition-wide position. I found no Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican material on this chapter.

---

## Part 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship and history (vv. 2–4, 9):**
- Bible Odyssey dates Sheshonq's attack to about 921 BC and treats the "Euphrates to Egypt" borders as an ideal rather than reality. https://biblehub.bibleodyssey.org/articles/the-divided-monarchy/
- The NET Bible's dictionary (quoting the ISBE) describes Shishak's own record at the Temple of Amon at Karnak. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php/xml/xml/dictionary.php?word=Shishak
- Hill dates the campaign to 925 BC and says it reached as far north as Megiddo. He argues that naming the Sukkites, who are known mainly from much earlier Egyptian records, shows the Chronicler used old sources. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary
- **Dates conflict:** Ellicott gives 949 BC, Hill 925 BC, Bible Odyssey about 921 BC.
- **Conflicting claims about Jerusalem:** One Precept Austin contributor says Shishak admitted he did not conquer Jerusalem. A Bible Hub article says only that the name doesn't appear in the surviving, damaged parts of the Karnak list. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-12-commentary ; https://biblehub.com/q/evidence_for_shishak's_invasion.htm
- Constable says the Chronicler's focus on immediate punishment warned his own community not to assume judgment would be delayed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/12-12.html

**Catholic and Orthodox:** I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. The only Catholic-related material is translation: the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims render the Sukkites as "Troglodytes" (v. 3), and the Vulgate reads v. 12 as "good works were found" in Judah, as Ellicott notes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/12-12.htm

**Prosperity, Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching:** Nothing found on the allowed sites for this chapter.
